metadata.title: Technical Design Collaboration Platform Residuality Stress Test
metadata.description: Explore how a technical-design platform would need to change when sensitive designs cannot use external AI, a repository provider ends critical integration access, a customer carves out a business unit, or regulated architecture knowledge must move under all three constraints.
metadata.naiveArchitecture: An engineer connects a code repository, asks an AI model to create or update a diagram and design document, collaborates with teammates in a workspace, and publishes or exports the approved artifact. The design assumes the AI processing path is allowed, repository links and events remain available, and workspace ownership and audience stay inside one company.
metadata.residualArchitecture: The changed design separates design intent, source artifact, source provider, retrieved snapshot, semantic architecture object, generated proposal, model and processing location, evidence, human decision, document, diagram, version, workspace, owning organization, access purpose, audience, reusable reference, export package, and revocation. A design can be regenerated through an approved model, remain current from portable source evidence, and move to a new organization without exposing unrelated knowledge.
metadata.note: These tests show that a diagram is not the architecture record by itself. The explicit change is to preserve sources, generated claims, human decisions, ownership, access scope, and publication history independently of any AI model, repository provider, or workspace boundary.

source.title: Residues: Time, Change, and Uncertainty in Software Architecture
source.author: Barry M. O'Reilly

stressors.name: Enterprise customers prohibit sensitive code and diagrams from reaching external AI models or training pipelines
stressors.detection: Customer contracts and policy, workspace and artifact classifications, connected source scope, prompts and retrieved context, model and provider inventory, processing and storage regions, training and retention settings, subprocessors, generated content, access logs, and security review.
stressors.attractor: AI generation is central to the experience, but the platform cannot prove which code and designs left the workspace, where they were processed, whether they influenced model training, or which generated claims came from sensitive context. Disabling AI removes value; treating a provider-level opt-out as sufficient leaves purpose and artifact scope unclear.
stressors.businessReaction: Classify content and permitted processing, offer approved regional or private model paths, minimize retrieved context, prevent training and excess retention, record model and subprocessor use, separate generated proposals from approved design facts, require review, support customer keys and deletion, and prove policy compliance per action.
stressors.residue: Separate user intent, workspace, source artifact, classification, selected context, prompt, model, model version, provider, processing location, retention and training policy, subprocessor, generated proposal, source citation, human review, accepted design change, access event, deletion task, and evidence. AI use is authorized for one purpose and content scope.

impacts.effect: Security leaders can permit useful AI design assistance without surrendering control of sensitive technical context.
Collaboration controls apply to the actual content, model path, purpose, retention, and generated result.
The workspace selects an allowed model and context path from classification, residency, training, retention, and customer-key policy.
A sensitive workspace counts as governed only when AI processing and generated-content access are included in its audited policy.
Adds content-aware model routing, context preview, processing labels, citations, review, customer controls, and deletion evidence.
Makes AI processing an explicit governed collaboration event rather than an invisible feature call.
Routes prompts by classification and policy and records context, model, version, provider, region, usage, and outcome.
Provides private and regional processing, customer-key controls, retention limits, deletion, and compliance evidence.
Scopes who may submit, view, approve, export, and reuse sensitive source and generated content.
Owns secure AI paths with authoring, model, infrastructure, identity, legal, sales, support, and customer-security teams.
Makes controllable AI processing for sensitive enterprise collaboration a category benchmark.

stressors.name: A dominant repository provider ends the API and event access used to keep architecture documents current
stressors.detection: Provider roadmap and contract notices, installed integrations and permissions, repositories and branches, webhook and API usage, cached snapshots, pull-request links, synchronization lag, monitor rules, customer alternatives, export formats, and support cases.
stressors.attractor: Living diagrams and design documents depend on provider-specific links, webhooks, comments, pull requests, and identifiers. When access disappears, documents still look current while their sources drift; a hurried migration loses history, review decisions, and the connection between a design claim and the code state that supported it.
stressors.businessReaction: Declare affected integrations, preserve the last verified source state and cursor, mark freshness honestly, obtain customer-directed exports, support alternate providers and local repositories, map identifiers, re-establish monitors and review links, reconcile missed changes, and retire inaccessible credentials and data.
stressors.residue: Separate repository concept, provider account, repository and branch identity, source snapshot, commit and change event, portable artifact manifest, ingestion cursor, semantic architecture claim, monitor, synchronization run, freshness state, drift finding, review link, provider adapter, migration mapping, and reconciliation result. Design currency no longer depends on one live provider URL.

impacts.effect: Staff engineers keep design knowledge tied to verifiable source states even when repository infrastructure changes.
Architecture documentation can remain current through provider migration rather than silently freezing.
Drift detection distinguishes verified current sources, missed event intervals, migrated identifiers, conflicts, and stale claims.
Trusted architecture communication includes the source snapshot and freshness limits behind each published claim.
Adds portable source manifests, adapter replacement, cursor transfer, missed-change reconciliation, and visible freshness.
Treats providers as replaceable sources while preserving source-to-design lineage and review state.
Separates repository identity and customer authorization from provider credentials, endpoints, and adapter state.
Versions source snapshots, cursors, mappings, proposed document changes, review decisions, conflicts, and reconciliation.
Reports source coverage and freshness and can rebind a monitor to migrated repositories and identifiers.
Owns provider exit with customers, repository vendors, integrations, data portability, authoring, review, security, and support.
Makes repository-neutral living documentation and migration a connected-workflow benchmark.

stressors.name: A customer divests a business unit and must transfer its architecture knowledge without exposing the remaining company
stressors.detection: Legal sale perimeter, organizations and workspace ownership, people and groups, systems and repositories, document and diagram references, shared libraries, comments and decisions, data classifications, contracts, access logs, dependencies, transition services, and buyer readiness.
stressors.attractor: Documents owned by the divested unit embed diagrams, comments, templates, links, code references, people, and dependencies from both sides. Copying whole workspaces leaks sensitive context; exporting only visible pages breaks references, provenance, review history, and the knowledge required to operate the acquired systems.
stressors.businessReaction: Define the knowledge perimeter, classify each artifact and reference, assign transfer, redact, duplicate, replace, or transition-service treatment, create buyer identities and ownership, preserve approved history and provenance, rebind sources, test usability, revoke seller access at cutover, and retain required evidence.
stressors.residue: Separate architecture object from document and diagram representation; artifact ownership from workspace location; reference from embedded copy; person from organization membership; access from transfer right; shared library element from customer customization; and source link from portable snapshot. Each item receives effective-dated transfer and disclosure treatment with provenance intact.

impacts.effect: Platform architects can assemble a usable architecture reference for a new organization without leaking the old one.
The buyer receives the key views, decisions, references, and current-source context needed to operate the divested systems.
Assembly shows transferred, redacted, duplicated, replaced, shared temporarily, and unresolved knowledge.
Audit requests can be answered from transferred provenance and access history without reconstructing the carve-out manually.
Adds knowledge-perimeter analysis, reference treatment, redaction, ownership transfer, portable packages, and buyer validation.
Preserves source, decision, diagram, document, and reference structure through selective organizational transfer.
Versions workspace organization, ownership, members, policy, transition, transfer scope, and cutover state.
Preserves approved history and provenance while creating redacted or transferred successor versions.
Identifies cross-boundary references and rebuilds the permitted knowledge graph for each resulting organization.
Owns selective knowledge transfer with customer architecture, transaction, security, legal, repository, identity, and support teams.
Makes governed architecture-knowledge carve-outs an enterprise diagramming and documentation benchmark.

stressors.name: A regulated service must transfer to the buyer after repository access ends and external AI processing is forbidden
stressors.detection: Sale and regulatory perimeter, service and data classifications, approved AI-processing policy, source manifests and last snapshots, repository migration mapping, design artifacts and references, ownership and audience, reviews and decisions, controls, buyer identities, export tests, and cutover evidence.
stressors.attractor: The buyer needs current, reviewable architecture evidence to operate a regulated service, but the original repository can no longer be queried, external AI cannot regenerate the views, and the seller cannot copy the surrounding workspace. A static PDF would lose source state, decision context, reusable references, and update capability.
stressors.businessReaction: Use the last verified source manifests, mark missing intervals, process only through an approved model path or manual review, select and redact the transfer perimeter, rebuild references and repository mappings for the buyer, review the design, publish a portable package, validate operation and audit use, and revoke seller-side access.
stressors.residue: No new structural change is required: content-aware AI policy provides an approved generation path, provider-neutral source lineage preserves currency and gaps, and selective ownership transfer creates a buyer-safe knowledge graph. Existing review and export components assemble the governed handover.

impacts.effect: Engineering leadership can complete a high-quality regulated handover despite model, repository, and organizational constraints.
Reviewers can approve the transferred design from explicit sources, gaps, decisions, controls, and ownership.
The final artifact includes portable source lineage, accepted decisions, open gaps, controls, references, and buyer ownership.
Review cycle time ends when the buyer receives an operable and auditable artifact, not when a file is exported.
Packages diagrams, documents, sources, decisions, references, permissions, and provenance for controlled transfer and embedding.
Reuses AI, source-lineage, and carve-out residues to conduct and preserve the buyer-seller review.
Produces a self-contained governed package with manifests, redactions, links, checksums, and access conditions.
Preserves scoped review questions, responses, resolutions, participants, and final decisions.
Carries only approved reusable patterns and creates buyer-owned successors for shared references.
Coordinates the handover across seller and buyer architects, security, compliance, repository, knowledge, identity, and transaction teams.
Makes portable, reviewable, policy-safe technical handover a professional collaboration benchmark.
